Based on my examination of the Flask codebase, here are the key files implementing the request pipeline and error handling:

`src/flask/app.py`

The WSGI entry point (`wsgi_app`) creates the context, calls `full_dispatch_request` to orchestrate the pipeline, catches exceptions to convert them to 500 responses via `handle_exception`, and ensures teardown happens in a finally block.

`src/flask/ctx.py`

The request context's `push` method sets up the request, opens the session, and matches the URL; the `pop` method calls teardown handlers and signals during cleanup.

`src/flask/signals.py`

Defines the signals sent at each stage: `request_started` (before preprocessing), `request_finished` (after finalization), `request_tearing_down` and `appcontext_tearing_down` (during teardown), and `got_request_exception` (when an exception occurs).

The complete flow: `wsgi_app` → `ctx.push()` → `request_started` signal → `preprocess_request` (before_request hooks) → `dispatch_request` (routing + handler execution) → exception caught by `handle_exception` which creates `InternalServerError` → `finalize_request` (response building + after_request hooks + `request_finished` signal) → `ctx.pop()` (teardown signals) → response sent. Unhandled exceptions are caught in `wsgi_app`'s except block and passed to `handle_exception`, which logs the error and returns a 500 `InternalServerError` response.

Based on my analysis of the Flask request pipeline, here are the key files implementing the request processing and error handling:

`src/flask/app.py:wsgi_app`
The WSGI entry point that creates the request context, calls full_dispatch_request, and catches exceptions at the top level to convert them to 500 responses.

`src/flask/app.py:full_dispatch_request`
Orchestrates the request flow: sends request_started signal, runs preprocess_request, dispatches to the view, handles exceptions with handle_user_exception, and finalizes with finalize_request.

`src/flask/app.py:preprocess_request`
Runs url_value_preprocessors and before_request hooks from app and blueprints in order, short-circuiting if any returns a non-None value.

`src/flask/app.py:handle_exception`
The catch-all handler that converts unhandled exceptions to InternalServerError (500), logs them, finds registered error handlers, and returns the response; re-raises in debug/testing mode if PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS is True.

`src/flask/ctx.py:pop`
The context cleanup method called in the wsgi_app finally block that invokes teardown_request handlers and ensures they always run even when errors occur.

The pipeline: `wsgi_app` → push context → `request_started` signal → `preprocess_request` (before_request) → `dispatch_request` (view) → `handle_user_exception` (if exception) → `finalize_request` (after_request, request_finished signal) → `pop` context (teardown_request) → convert unhandled exceptions to 500 in `handle_exception` → return response.

`src/flask/app.py`

This file implements the entire request pipeline: `wsgi_app()` is the WSGI entry point that creates the request context and calls `full_dispatch_request()`, which orchestrates `preprocess_request()` (before_request hooks), `dispatch_request()` (view execution), and `finalize_request()` (after_request hooks); unhandled exceptions are caught and passed to `handle_exception()` which creates an `InternalServerError` and converts it to a 500 response via `finalize_request()`.

`src/flask/ctx.py`

This file defines the `AppContext` class whose `push()` and `pop()` methods manage the request context lifecycle; `pop()` is called after the response is finalized to run teardown handlers and signals regardless of whether an error occurred.

Based on my analysis of the Flask source code, here are the files implementing the request handling pipeline:

`src/flask/app.py`
This file contains the core WSGI request handling: `wsgi_app` (entry point), `full_dispatch_request` (orchestrates pre-processing, dispatch, and post-processing), `preprocess_request` (runs before_request hooks and url_value_preprocessors), `dispatch_request` (matches routing and calls the view), `process_response` (runs after_request hooks and saves sessions), and `finalize_request` (converts return values to responses).

`src/flask/ctx.py`
The `AppContext.push()` and `AppContext.pop()` methods manage the request context lifecycle, sending signals and calling teardown functions that run after the response is prepared.

`src/flask/app.py`
The `handle_exception` method (called when exceptions escape the dispatch chain) is responsible for converting unhandled errors to 500 responses: it sends the `got_request_exception` signal, logs the exception, wraps it in an `InternalServerError`, checks for registered 500 error handlers, and calls `finalize_request` to convert it to a response.

`src/flask/app.py`
The `handle_user_exception` method handles exceptions raised by views and before_request hooks, routing HTTPExceptions to proper handlers and re-raising others for `handle_exception` to catch.

Based on my analysis of the Flask codebase, here are the files that implement reusable groups of routes (blueprints) mounted with URL prefixes and nested group support:

`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`
This file contains the core blueprint registration logic, including nested blueprint mounting with combined URL prefixes and duplicate name validation.

`src/flask/sansio/app.py`
The Flask app's register_blueprint method delegates to the blueprint's register method, initiating the registration process.

`src/flask/blueprints.py`
The Flask-specific Blueprint wrapper that extends SansioBlueprint with Flask-specific functionality like CLI integration.

Looking at the blueprint registration logic, here are the key files:

`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`
Implements `Blueprint.register()` method which handles duplicate name rejection (raises ValueError if `name in app.blueprints`), nested blueprint registration with URL prefix merging, and recursive registration loop.

`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`
Contains `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule()` which applies the URL prefix to routes using path joining logic.

`src/flask/sansio/app.py`
Provides `App.register_blueprint()` entry point that delegates to the blueprint's register method.

`src/flask/helpers.py`
Implements `_split_blueprint_path()` utility that recursively splits dotted blueprint names to resolve nested blueprint hierarchies.

`src/flask/blueprints.py`
Public wrapper module that re-exports the Blueprint class from sansio.

`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`

This file implements the `Blueprint` class with the `register_blueprint` method (line 256) for mounting nested groups, the `register` method (line 273) that concatenates URL prefixes for nested blueprints and rejects duplicate names by checking `app.blueprints` dictionary (lines 306-314), and handles nested blueprint URL prefix composition (lines 364-374).

`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`

The `Blueprint.register()` method (line 273) handles mounting nested blueprints with concatenated URL prefixes (lines 364-377) and checks for duplicate names in `app.blueprints` (lines 306-314), raising `ValueError` if the same name is registered twice.
